extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly; naturalists, botanists, and educated general public interested in plant physiology
extracted.subtask_description: A magazine review and exposition of Charles Darwin's experimental work on the spontaneous and modified movements of plants (circumnutation, nyctitropism, etc.), describing methods, observations, definitions, and interpretations. Geared to explaining the experiments, results, and biological significance to an informed non-specialist audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for recording organ movement (glass filament and bead tracing)
rubrics_metrics.description: A glass filament (horse-hair thickness, 1/4 to 3/4 inch long) is affixed to the organ, with a minute bead of black sealing-wax at its end; a dot on a card behind the bead is viewed through a horizontal glass plate, and when the bead exactly covers the dot a mark is made on the glass. Other dots are made at short intervals and afterward joined by straight lines to show movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details: filament attached with shellac dissolved in alcohol (sets in 2–3 seconds); weight light enough not to press leaves; dots at short intervals produce angular tracings (more frequent dots would give more curved lines); example magnification: filament ~3/4 in, bead 1/2 in from card, glass 7 in in front → movement magnified ~15×. Night movements shown by broken lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative tracing method (tracing-paper magnification)
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative method copies the dots from the glass plate onto tracing-paper, joining them with ruled lines and arrows to show direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the first dot larger to catch the eye; this method is preferable when greater magnification or clearer directional indication is required; night movements may be indicated with broken lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of circumnutation
rubrics_metrics.description: Circumnutation: the spontaneous, ever-present rotating/nodding movement (revolving nutation) of growing parts of plants — stems, tendrils, radicles, leaves, etc. — considered a universal property of growing vegetation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin's evidence: observed in buried stems and rootlets of germinating seeds; diagrams and long-term tracings across many genera; circumnutation consists typically of irregular narrow ellipses with zigzags, loops, and varying rates (from one ellipse a day to four or five).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: nutation vs circumnutation
rubrics_metrics.description: Nutation historically meant nodding (e.g., flower following sun); Darwin suggests 'circumnutation' as a better term for the revolving/rotating spontaneous movement found broadly in plants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circumnutation emphasizes the revolving aspect and universal presence in growing parts rather than simple nodding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental conditions for observing movements
rubrics_metrics.description: Plants should be grown in pots and protected from or illuminated in controlled ways (totally from above, from one side, etc.), often covered by a horizontal glass sheet and sometimes a vertical sheet to permit observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep proper temperature; use darkness or feeble illumination when required; secure stems to a stick near the leaf base when observing leaf movements; many observations used ground glass illumination to standardize light; conditions of moisture and temperature strongly affect nyctitropic movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nyctitropic movement (sleep) criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A movement is nyctitropic (the 'sleep' of leaves) only if it has been acquired for the purpose of diminishing loss of heat by radiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin sets an arbitrary angular threshold of 60° above or below the horizon as a practical limit: any smaller rise/fall is of slight significance for radiation protection. Nyctitropic behavior is also judged by whether it is widespread in the genus and affected predictably by light/dark cycles and hereditary habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seat and plane of leaf movement
rubrics_metrics.description: The seat of movement in leaves is generally in the petiole, though sometimes in the blade; the movement is chiefly in a vertical plane but usually includes some lateral motion, producing irregular ellipses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observations across 30–40 genera support this; when measuring, secure stem to a stick near the leaf base to isolate petiole movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation: movements are modifications of an intrinsic process
rubrics_metrics.description: Pressure, light, gravitation and other irritants do not directly cause movement but modify spontaneous changes in cell turgescence and cell-wall extensibility; circumnutation is the universal consequence of these internal rhythmic changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use experiments that isolate external factors to show modification vs direct causation; consider rhythmical periods of rest in cells as a possible mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement of microscale jerks
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the microscope some movements are composed of sudden small jerks forward of about 0.002 or 0.001 inch followed by slow retreat; such jerking was notable in a few cases but not detected with a two-inch object-glass in Drosera.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Microscopical detection requires appropriate magnification and sensitive setups; it is unclear how general such jerks are — require replication across species and organs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional criterion for radicle circumnutation
rubrics_metrics.description: Circumnutation of radicles is useful at least in enabling the tip to take the line of least resistance and may aid descent into crevices, old worm burrows, or holes made by larvae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin's observations include radicles following old burrows and experiments showing how tip behavior aids penetration; interpret usefulness by observing radicle interactions with heterogenous substrates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative force measurements of radicle growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Growing radicles increase in thickness and can exert transverse forces: at least a quarter of a pound when free to bend, and much greater when prevented from bending; specific experiments required 8 lb 8 oz or 3 lb 4 oz to re-open fissures/pincers previously widened by radicle growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental setups: radicle grown through split stick or holes in spring-closing pincers placed in damp sand, then force required to open the split/pincers measured after removing radicle. These force values provide quantitative evidence of mechanical work by roots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling breadth as a classificatory standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Darwin's conclusions are supported by observations across many genera and families: seedlings (many diagrams), about 20 genera for mature-plant circumnutation tests, 30–40 genera for leaves, and nyctitropic positions for 153 genera of cotyledons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use wide, taxonomically diverse sampling when claiming universality or generality of a movement/habit; report numbers and selection reasons for included genera.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational tracing and representation conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Tracings from glass-dot marks are joined by straight lines (thus angular); more frequent dots produce smoother curves; night movements may be indicated by broken lines; first dot may be enlarged/circled to indicate start and direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about sampling interval, magnification factor, and line conventions when publishing tracings; indicate day vs night and arrowheads for direction.
